questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Other

questions.question: Please explain: *
questions.answer: It's been a huge motivation for me to go on exchange after hearing from so many students from Molecular Biomedicine how it's been the best decision they ever made. I wanted to go abroad for all of the listed options, non in particular - both academic and career opportunities, and exploring new cultures and people.

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: One of my best friends went on exchange to Australia when she was 15 and has felt ever since that it's been her second home. It's been a motivation for me since then to visit the place that means so much to one of my closest. Additionally, I've spoken to several friends and family friends who've visited the west and east coast of Australia, telling me how the west coast is much less touristy, un-spoiled, and has so much beautiful nature. I come from a small town in Denmark and have always appreciated nature, water, open spaces, chill vibes and people. And I'm not much of a big city person so Perth and the authentic west coast was very appealing to me. I looked up universities on the west coast and found that UWA had several units I found very interesting, so everything worked out.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Everything was available online but if anything was unclear or difficult to find I found that everyone I asked was very eager to help.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: A well-organized orientation week with plenty of opportunities to ask for any help you might need. Guides to online access to everything you needed to know, unit enrollment, schedule management etc. was provided throughout the week, and you were familiarized with several orientation week organizers whom you could ask anything.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: Some of the content during the orientation week was a bit unnecessary but overall it was a great way to meet other international students and definitely worth attending.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I read other travel reports from previous years that said that it was very easy and cheap to find accommodation upon arrival and they recommended to not make any arrangements prior to arrival. However, I found the exact opposite since this year was the first since COVID-19 where international students were allowed in WA. This meant that Perth was booming with international students (and other internationals traveling, or moving to Perth for work etc.) like never before and finding accommodation was hectic. So when I was offered a room in an apartment I just accepted.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer:
I lived in the CBD which truly sucked. Perth is amazing but you definitely want to stay in one of the suburbs. The CBD has a weird vibe and it doesn't have much charm. It was easy to get to uni, and it's close to the bus and train station but I didn't make use of either very often anyways. I stayed at The Switch which was alright but quite expensive ($295 per week) but there was nice common areas, a shared kitchen, rooftop terraces, study areas, the Study Perth organization on the ground floor (you could print for free here, very nice!), and a small gym which made it very convenient. And it's close to a nice neighborhood called 'Northbridge' which is basically Perth's equivalent to Nørrebro in Copenhagen, super nice. But I'd definitely look for a shared house by the beach somewhere which would've made the experience much more 'Australian'. Talk to people, look on Facebook Marketplace, flatmates etc.. The suburbs are truly charming, especially Scarborough and Fremantle.

Huge pro tip: There are a handful of free buses in Perth called 'Cat' busses; e.g. the Purple Cat drives from the CBD to both the main campus and the health campus which was super convenient! You can also get a TransPerth card for public transportation when you have to go places where the free buses don't drive and you get a student discount, so the public transportation is a very small expense.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It's also a possibility to stay at one of the colleges near campus, they were just veeery expensive. But everyone I know who stayed there has been so happy about their choice. However, it's a big commitment since there are a lot of events for the college students and that will probably be your primary 'socialization circle'. And you have to apply for this in advance.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Online enrollment was very intuitive but you had to allocate yourself into different classes which was a bit confusing at first. But I found that it was very helpful to just have a chat with someone from the global/international students office. Just ask around and you get the help you need for anything!

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: You had to enroll in units online which was super easy. Afterwards you had to make your own schedule which was quite nice since you can just plan your week like you want to.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Online guides, staff from the orientation week and at the office on campus, and you could also just send an e-mail.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: Completely. I originally wanted two units which I was denied but when I talked to one of the coordinators from the orientation week I was accepted into the units anyways. Super easy!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just ask around if you have any questions, everyone's eager to help!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was enrolled in two units which were part of a Master's course at the Health Campus. I just didn't know that the units were part of this course and that it was a diagnostic course which I do not find interesting at all. Maybe I could've found more information about this if I had just payed more attention, who knows. But this was also a 'special case' since my exchange was during my master's due to COVID-19 and I had to follow two units equivalent to the compulsory Molecular Pathology at UCPH. Usually you don't have to worry about compulsory units since there's more elective units in the bachelor program.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Generally a bit easier than units at UCPH, I'd say. But the workload during the semester was definitely heavier since there were continuous assessment, quizzes, mid-semester exams etc. which made it a lot more stressful compared to UCPH. But this also forced you to keep up with the curriculum which was quite nice and made the study break for final exams lighter.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was quite different due to the continuous assessments, and in general it was much more high school-like since students are also graded on class participation which really removes the 'self-study' component that most students from UCPH are used to. I didn't really like it but some people do. However, this also made the teachers more engaged and 'personal' than back home which was really nice.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: PATH5151 Molecular Pathology, PATH5131 Anatomical Pathology, APHB5503 Neuroendocrinology, SSEH1104 Active Leadership (SUP)

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: If you're interested in diagnostics, both molecular pathology and anatomical pathology are quite nice. I especially enjoyed the lab work in anatomical pathology where we made our own slide sections and histology stainings. These are only offered to master's students though. The content of neuroendocrinology was super interesting but the teaching was a bit unstructured, unfortunately. The final essay was a nice wrap up for the unit contents but this unit is also only offered to master's students. Active leadership is an undergrad unit which was super easy and a great way to meet new people. The workload was super light and it was super fun to do stand up paddleboarding (you could chose kayaking or mountainbiking as well) and all you had to do was to solve some challenges within your team. Highly recommend this unit to also be able to focus more on other units and to give yourself a break during the week.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I bought a car with three other Danish girls. We got one really cheap ($2000) on Facebook Marketplace but a car comes with quite a lot of expenses, e.g. just the gas! However, this was the best buy I made while I was in Perth.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Housing was more expensive than expected. Coffee was super cheap compared to Copenhagen so I ended up spending much more money on coffee than back home but it was a really nice luxury!

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Free introduction courses for different sports were offered to international students, as well as 1 month for free at the gym on campus. However, the introduction sessions were during the 'school day' so I always had classes. We heard a lot about different clubs but it didn't really seem like it was something that people actually made use of which was a shame. And it was quite difficult to join a sports team, nobody could tell me how to join a volleyball team even though I asked several different people.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Don't really know.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Buy a car (if you're staying the entire semester, otherwise rent one for a weekend) and go on heaps of roadtrips and explore WA, that's what makes the whole thing worth it!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Very easy. Australians are super friendly and welcoming in general.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Staying at the colleges is probably the best way, or maybe being very consistent in making an effort to speak to local students at uni. It's not very common for students in Australia to make friends at uni since most people hang out with their friends from middle/high school!

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Maybe the fact that Australians don't make friends at uni very often. However, the international students were very eager to make friends and if you're open to it you can definitely make some friends for life at uni, most likely just not the locals.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The people. I love the people. And I love how multicultural Perth is and how there's room for everyone everywhere. The Australian way of everyone just being kind, open-minded, welcoming, thoughtful, and super polite. I felt that it motivated me to act in the same way and always just lifted my mood. Meeting so many different people have definitely been the best part of my exchange stay.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Be mindful of the continuous assessments for better and for worse - it's gonna help you out in the end even though it might be stressful during the semester. Be openminded - ask around for which ever questions you might have, be open to meeting new people. Buy a car!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: The weather in Perth was not as I (or any other exchange students) expected. It was very rainy for almost the entire semester, especially the first months. Two pairs of long pants was not enough. They told us that the weather wasn't usually like that but I don't know if I believe them! I'd say to not count on the weather to be summer-like until the end of the semester. Bring a raincoat and an umbrella, it'll come in handy. Of course there are sunny days as well but I was definitely expecting there to be many more sunny days from the beginning.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Being overwhelmed by so many new impressions but still finding a balance between uni, figuring out who was my people and who were just nice acquaintances, keeping up with the continuous assessments but also wanting to go on roadtrips every chance that I got, adjusting to a new city and always trying to get the most of every experience, but also needing to take a breather at times. And having said this, traveling along the entire west coast in our car, especially down south, with everything this included has definitely been what made my exchange stay so fantastic. Spending so much time with these people in the car, exploring the beautiful nature, meeting so many interesting people.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Finding a balance. I found that I had to be very aware of when I was challenged in a good way and when I was too overwhelmed by everything, especially during the first month with new impressions and during periods at uni with many deadlines. But this was also part of what made it all worth it. Talk to people about what you're experiencing, most of them will feel the same way or at least be able to relate and understand!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Go-go-go on exchange, it's the best decision I've ever made. And if you appreciate beautiful nature and quiet spaces, Perth and WA is the place to be. It's the most beautiful place I've ever visited. Sunsets in Perth just hits differently (and you can't watch the sunset on the east coast:))!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
